title: Microscopy
aim: To use a light microscope to observe, draw and label onion epidermal cells, and to estimate the real size of a cell using magnification.
background: A light microscope uses lenses to magnify an image of a thin specimen. Light from a lamp or mirror passes up through the specimen, then through the objective lens and the eyepiece lens to your eye. The total magnification is the eyepiece magnification multiplied by the objective magnification, so a ×10 eyepiece with a ×40 objective gives a total magnification of ×400.

Onion epidermis is a good specimen because it is only one cell thick, so light can pass through it and the cells do not overlap. The cells are colourless, so a stain such as iodine solution is added to increase contrast. Iodine stains the nucleus and cell wall yellow-brown so they stand out. Onion bulb cells do not contain chloroplasts because the bulb grows underground and does not photosynthesise.

Once the cells have been observed, their real size can be estimated. One way is to measure the diameter of the field of view with a clear ruler at low power, count how many cells fit across it, then divide. Another is to use the magnification equation: real size = image size ÷ magnification. Sizes of cells are usually given in micrometres (μm), where 1 mm = 1000 μm.
hypothesis: Onion epidermal cells will appear as roughly rectangular, box-shaped cells with a cell wall, cytoplasm and a nucleus, and each cell will be roughly 100 to 300 μm long.

variables.independent: Magnification used (objective lens: ×4, ×10 or ×40), which changes how many cells are seen and how much detail is visible.
variables.dependent: The structures that can be seen and the estimated size of one cell (μm).
control: Same type of specimen (epidermis from the inner surface of the same onion scale leaf)
Same stain and the same amount of stain (one or two drops of iodine solution)
Specimen kept as a single, flat layer of cells with no air bubbles

equipment: Light microscope with ×10 eyepiece and ×4, ×10 and ×40 objective lenses
Scalpel or knife and white tile
Clear plastic ruler marked in mm
Sharp pencil and plain paper for drawing
method: Use a pipette to put one drop of water onto the centre of a clean microscope slide.
Cut a piece of onion and separate one of the fleshy scale leaves. Use forceps to peel off a thin layer of epidermal tissue from the inner (concave) surface.
Use the forceps to lay the epidermis flat on the drop of water on the slide, smoothing out any folds so it is a single layer of cells.
Add one or two drops of iodine solution to the onion tissue to stain it.
Hold a coverslip at an angle at one edge of the specimen and use a mounted needle to lower it slowly onto the tissue. This stops air bubbles being trapped under the coverslip.
Use a paper towel to soak up any excess liquid from around the edge of the coverslip.
Place the slide on the microscope stage and hold it in place with the stage clips. Switch on the lamp.
Select the lowest power objective lens (×4). Looking from the side, use the coarse focusing knob to move the stage up until the slide is just below the objective lens.
Looking down the eyepiece, use the coarse focusing knob to move the stage slowly away from the lens until the cells come into focus.
Use the fine focusing knob to make the image sharp. Move the slide so the cells you want to look at are in the centre of the field of view.
Switch to a higher power objective lens (×10, then ×40) and refocus using only the fine focusing knob.
Make a clear, labelled pencil drawing of a few cells, and write the total magnification next to the drawing.

To estimate cell size, switch back to the ×10 objective, place a clear ruler on the stage and measure the diameter of the field of view in mm. Replace the ruler with the slide, count how many cells fit end to end across the diameter, and repeat in five different fields of view.

safety.risk: Can irritate the eyes and stains skin and clothing.
safety.precaution: Wear eye protection, use only one or two drops, and wash off any splashes on skin with water.

safety.risk: Cuts to fingers when cutting the onion.
safety.precaution: Cut on a white tile, cut away from the body and keep fingers clear of the blade.

safety.risk: Cuts from broken or chipped glass; coverslips are very thin and break easily.
safety.precaution: Handle by the edges, never use the coarse focus at high power so the lens does not crush the slide, and report breakages so the glass can be cleared up safely.

safety.risk: The bulb can become hot and could cause a burn; mains electricity near water.
safety.precaution: Do not touch the bulb, keep water away from the plug and lamp, and switch off when finished.

headers: Diameter of field of view at ×100 (μm)
results.notes: The field of view diameter was measured as 1.8 mm with a clear ruler, which is 1800 μm. Estimated cell length = diameter of field of view ÷ number of cells across it. The mean estimated length is (225 + 200 + 257 + 225 + 225) ÷ 5 = 226 μm (to 3 significant figures). A labelled drawing at ×400 should show box-shaped cells with a cell wall, cytoplasm, a nucleus and a large vacuole, and no chloroplasts.

analysis: Onion epidermal cells appear as long, roughly rectangular cells arranged in rows like bricks. At ×400 the cell wall, cytoplasm and a stained nucleus are clearly visible. The large permanent vacuole takes up most of the cell but is hard to see because it is colourless. No chloroplasts are seen because the onion bulb is not exposed to light and does not photosynthesise.

The mean estimated length of one cell is about 226 μm, which is within the expected range of 100 to 300 μm for onion epidermal cells. Taking a mean of five fields of view reduces the effect of any one unusual count.

The magnification equation can be used to find real size from a drawing or photograph: real size = image size ÷ magnification. For example, if a cell is drawn 90 mm long and the drawing is at ×400, the real length is 90 ÷ 400 = 0.225 mm = 225 μm, which agrees with the field of view estimate.

Higher magnification shows more detail of fewer cells, but a light microscope cannot resolve structures smaller than about 0.2 μm, so ribosomes and the detailed structure of mitochondria cannot be seen. These need an electron microscope.

errors.error: Air bubbles trapped under the coverslip hide cells or are mistaken for cells.
errors.improvement: Lower the coverslip slowly at an angle using a mounted needle, and recognise bubbles as round, dark-edged circles that are not part of the specimen.

errors.error: The epidermis is folded or more than one cell thick, so cells overlap and are hard to count.
errors.improvement: Peel a thinner piece of epidermis and flatten it carefully in the drop of water before adding the coverslip.

errors.error: Cells do not fit an exact whole number of times across the field of view, so the count is only an estimate.
errors.improvement: Count cells in several fields of view and calculate a mean, or use a calibrated eyepiece graticule for more precise measurements.

errors.error: The field of view diameter measured with a ruler is imprecise because the ruler only reads to the nearest 1 mm.
errors.improvement: Measure the field of view at the lowest power, where several mm divisions are visible, and calculate the diameter at higher power by scaling, or use a stage micrometer.

examTips: Always start on the lowest power objective lens, then move to higher power. At high power use only the fine focusing knob.
Learn the magnification equation and how to rearrange it: real size = image size ÷ magnification. Convert both sizes to the same unit before dividing (1 mm = 1000 μm).
Biological drawings: use a sharp pencil, clear continuous lines, no shading, label lines drawn with a ruler that touch the structure, and state the magnification.
Do not label chloroplasts on onion epidermis cells: the bulb grows underground and its cells have none.
Magnification has no units, but you can write it with a × sign, for example ×400.

questions.question:
A student added a few drops of iodine solution to onion epidermis on a microscope slide.
Why did the student add iodine solution?
options: To kill the cells so they stop moving
To stain structures such as the nucleus so they can be seen more clearly
To stop the cells drying out
To make the cells bigger so they are easier to see
markScheme: 1 mark: to stain structures (such as the nucleus or cell wall) and increase contrast
questions.explanation: Onion epidermis cells are almost colourless, so they are hard to see. Iodine stains the nucleus and cell wall, increasing contrast. Onion cells do not move, and the stain does not change their size. Water, not iodine, stops the tissue drying out.

questions.question: Which objective lens should a student use first when viewing a new slide?
options: ×40, because it shows the most detail
×10, because it is in the middle of the range
×100, because it gives the highest magnification
×4, because it is the lowest power and gives the widest field of view
markScheme: 1 mark: ×4 (the lowest power objective)
questions.explanation: The lowest power objective shows the largest area of the slide, so it is easiest to find the cells and focus. It also leaves the most space between lens and slide, so the slide is not damaged. You then move up to higher power once the cells are centred.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the magnification of the lenses used on a light microscope.
Calculate the total magnification.
questions.explanation: Total magnification = eyepiece magnification × objective magnification = 10 × 40 = 400. A common mistake is to add the two values (giving 50) instead of multiplying.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows a student's drawing of an onion cell.
The real length of the cell is 0.12 mm.
Calculate the magnification of the drawing.
Use the equation:
magnification = size of image ÷ size of real object

markScheme: 1 mark: magnification = image size ÷ real size = 36 ÷ 0.12
1 mark: ×300
questions.explanation: Both lengths are already in mm, so divide directly: 36 ÷ 0.12 = 300. Dividing the wrong way round (0.12 ÷ 36) gives a number smaller than 1, which cannot be right for a drawing that is bigger than the real cell.

questions.question:
A student took a photograph of an onion cell through a light microscope.
Table 1 shows information about the photograph.
Calculate the real length of the cell in micrometres (μm).
1 mm = 1000 μm

rows: Length of the cell in the photograph in mm

markScheme: 1 mark: real size = image size ÷ magnification = 45 ÷ 150
1 mark: = 0.3 mm
questions.explanation: Real size = 45 ÷ 150 = 0.3 mm. To convert mm to μm multiply by 1000, giving 300 μm. Students often forget to convert units, giving 0.3 as their final answer.

questions.question: Explain why the student must use a very thin layer of onion epidermis on the slide.
markScheme: 1 mark: so light can pass through the specimen
1 mark: so it is a single layer of cells and cells do not overlap, making individual cells visible
questions.explanation: A light microscope works by shining light up through the specimen. If the tissue is thick, too little light passes through and overlapping cells make the image unclear.

questions.question: Give one reason why the coverslip is lowered onto the specimen slowly and at an angle.
markScheme: 1 mark: to avoid trapping air bubbles under the coverslip
questions.explanation: Air bubbles look like dark-edged circles and can hide cells or be mistaken for them. Lowering the coverslip from one side pushes the air out as the liquid spreads.

questions.question: Which structure would a student not see in onion epidermis cells viewed at ×400?
markScheme: 1 mark: chloroplast
questions.explanation: Onion epidermis cells are plant cells, so they have a cell wall, nucleus and cytoplasm. However, the onion bulb grows underground and does not photosynthesise, so its cells have no chloroplasts. Many students wrongly assume all plant cells contain chloroplasts.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows the field of view when a student looked at onion cells with a light microscope at ×100.
The diameter of the field of view is 1.8 mm.
Use Figure 1 to estimate the length of one cell in μm.
1 mm = 1000 μm
markScheme: 1 mark: 1.8 mm = 1800 μm
1 mark: 6 cells across the diameter, so 1800 ÷ 6 = 300 μm
questions.explanation: Count the cells lying end to end across the widest part of the field of view: there are 6. Convert the diameter to micrometres first (1.8 × 1000 = 1800 μm), then divide by the number of cells: 1800 ÷ 6 = 300 μm.

options: The coarse focusing knob only works at low power
The fine focusing knob makes the image bigger
The coarse focusing knob changes the magnification
The lens is very close to the slide, and a large movement could crash the lens into the slide
markScheme: 1 mark: the objective is very close to the slide so the coarse knob could break the slide or damage the lens
questions.explanation: At high power the gap between the objective and the slide is very small. The coarse knob moves the stage a long way, so it could push the slide into the lens. Neither knob changes magnification; they only change focus.

questions.question: Give three rules a student should follow when making a scientific drawing of cells seen under a microscope.
markScheme: 1 mark each, up to 3: use a sharp pencil; clear, continuous outlines with no shading or sketchy lines; label lines drawn with a ruler that touch the structure and do not cross; state the magnification; draw only what is actually seen; give the drawing a title; take up a reasonable amount of the space
questions.explanation: Scientific drawings are meant to be accurate records, not artistic pictures. Shading and sketchy lines make structures unclear, and including the magnification allows the real size to be calculated.

questions.question:
A student measured the lengths of four onion epidermal cells.
Table 1 shows the results.
Calculate the mean length of the cells in metres.
Give your answer in standard form.
1 m = 1 000 000 μm
questions.explanation: First calculate the mean: 900 ÷ 4 = 225 μm. There are 10⁶ μm in a metre, so divide by 1 000 000: 225 ÷ 1 000 000 = 0.000225 m, which is 2.25 × 10⁻⁴ m in standard form.

questions.question:
A student estimated the length of onion cells by counting the cells across the field of view in only one place on the slide.
Suggest why this estimate might not be representative.
Suggest how the estimate could be improved.
acceptedAnswers: repeat in different fields of view
markScheme: 1 mark: cells vary in size, so one area may contain unusually large or small cells
1 mark: count cells in several different fields of view and calculate a mean
questions.explanation: Biological material is variable. Repeating the count in several places and calculating a mean reduces the effect of any one unusual area and gives a more representative estimate.

questions.question: Describe how a student could prepare a slide of onion epidermis cells and use a light microscope to observe the cells clearly at high magnification.
markScheme: Indicative content: put a drop of water on a clean slide; peel a thin layer of epidermis from the inner surface of an onion scale leaf with forceps; lay it flat on the water without folds; add a drop of iodine solution to stain; lower the coverslip at an angle with a mounted needle to avoid air bubbles; blot excess liquid; place slide on stage and secure with clips; use lowest power objective first; use coarse focus (moving stage away from the lens) to focus; then fine focus; centre the cells; switch to higher power objective and refocus with fine focus only; calculate total magnification = eyepiece × objective

Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a detailed, coherent method in a logical order covering both slide preparation and use of the microscope, including staining and avoiding air bubbles, and starting at low power before moving to high power with fine focus.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a method covering most stages of slide preparation and microscope use, with some detail missing or steps slightly out of order.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements about preparing a slide or using a microscope, lacking logical order.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: A top answer works through the practical in order: preparing a thin, stained specimen without air bubbles, then focusing at low power before moving to high power with the fine focus. Missing out the stain, the coverslip technique, or the low-to-high power sequence are the most common reasons for losing marks.

questions.question: A student viewed onion cells at ×400 and wanted to see the ribosomes and the internal structure of the mitochondria. Explain why the student could not see these structures, and what type of microscope would be needed.
markScheme: Indicative content: ribosomes and mitochondrial detail are very small (ribosomes about 20 to 30 nm); a light microscope has limited resolution (about 200 nm); structures closer together or smaller than this cannot be distinguished; increasing magnification alone does not increase detail; an electron microscope is needed; it uses a beam of electrons with a much shorter wavelength, giving much higher resolution (about 0.1 nm) and magnification
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear explanation linking the small size of the structures to the limited resolution of the light microscope, and stating that an electron microscope has higher resolution.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): states that the structures are too small, or that an electron microscope is needed, with little explanation.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: The key idea is resolution, not just magnification. A light microscope image could be magnified further but would just become blurry. Electron microscopes have much higher resolving power, so they reveal sub-cellular structures such as ribosomes.
